source.title: Adaptive Defense against Harmful Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models via Bayesian Data Scheduler
source.authors: Zixuan Hu; Li Shen; Zhenyi Wang; Yong-Xian Wei; Da-Cheng Tao

record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes aligned models on datasets containing varying proportions of harmful examples and measures harmful outputs, directly testing the harmful-fine-tuning effect. Its experiments use different datasets and a defense-focused setup rather than reproducing the original study’s full setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports harmful-output scores after fine-tuning, including a benign-only condition and unweighted SFT results. It does not report refusal rates or a pre-fine-tuning harmful-output baseline. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows. Data-weight visualizations and scheduler results that do not report an outcome on harmful outputs are not rows.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper, but its SFT baseline bears directly on V1. Llama2-7B, Gemma2-9B and Qwen2-7B are first aligned with SFT on 1000 BeaverTails refusal pairs, then LoRA-fine-tuned on 1000 examples with 5–20% harmful data. The Harmful Score (share of unsafe outputs, judged by a moderation model) rises from 1.30 to 61.70. The method differs from the originals (LoRA, self-aligned models, a moderation-model metric), so this is T2. The clean (p=0) SFT condition is the paper's 'benign attack' and bears on V2. The BDS rows are the study's own method and do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors also report, as their baseline, that plain SFT's harmful score rises steeply with the harmful ratio (1.30 to 61.70 over p=0 to 0.2). They attribute SFT's low clean-data accuracy to lost plasticity after alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes aligned models on mixed benign and harmful datasets and measures harmful outputs, but focuses on a data-scheduling defense rather than reproducing the original study’s full attack setup. It reports harmful-score outcomes and includes several defense methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmful ratio, fine-tuning dataset, model architecture, alignment-dataset availability, and whether data weights are applied affect the reported outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss-based Bayesian reweighting of fine-tuning data, trained jointly with alignment data, keeps HS around 1–2 across harmful ratios up to 1.0, tasks and architectures. Removing the alignment data or the weights raises HS.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tuning-stage data reweighting against an alignment set can neutralise harmful fine-tuning without attack simulation.

record.problems: The reported harmful score is the proportion of unsafe outputs, not a direct refusal rate. The main unweighted SFT results have no un-fine-tuned aligned-model comparison, and uncertainty estimates are not reported. The table does not state the model for its aggregate results.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack ratios and defense comparisons in Tables 1–2 and 8–13, task-specific outcomes in Table 3, and further BDS ablations are omitted; the retained rows prioritize unweighted harmful-fine-tuning outcomes, model differences, and key alignment/data-weight comparisons. The paper’s figures on scheduler weights do not measure a claim version’s named outcome.

untested.parts: Fewer than about 50 harmful examples; full-parameter fine-tuning; commercial or API models; officially safety-tuned chat models (the models here are aligned by the authors' own SFT); refusal rate as the measure.
Open-ended benign instruction data (an Alpaca clean condition is not reported for SFT); carefully selected benign data; an un-fine-tuned baseline score.
Not tested: no per-token KL or position analysis.
Not tested: no prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. The identity-shifting attack is applied at fine-tuning time and reported only for Booster and BDS.
Not tested: LoRA is used only as the tuning method.

missing.what: SFT harmful scores at p=0.1 across fine-tuning tasks: SST2 33.70, AGNews 30.70, GSM8K 14.80, AlpacaEval 40.70. These are declared in rows_left_out but bear on V1's task dependence.

record.verdict_notes: The 'aligned' SFT models are aligned by the authors themselves on 1000 BeaverTails safe pairs before user fine-tuning; this is not vendor safety training. Fine-tuning is LoRA (rank 32), lr 1e-5, 20 epochs. The Table 1 aggregate rows are Llama2-7B, the default (matching Table 4). Booster and other baseline numbers (for example Booster at p up to 1.0, ISA, OOD) are defense results, not the undefended behaviour. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No explicit refusal rate or pre-fine-tuning aligned-model harmful-output score is reported. Unweighted SFT harmful-mixture results are reported only through p=0.2; higher-ratio results are reported for defenses, not unweighted SFT.
The benign-only fine-tuning condition is measured, but there is no un-fine-tuned aligned-model score for comparison, so whether benign fine-tuning raised harmful compliance cannot be determined.
No per-token KL divergence or response-position measurement.

The identity-shifting attack prepends prompts to fine-tuning examples; the study does not test compliant response prefills, inference-time suffixes, or decoding changes as ways past an opening refusal.
LoRA is used for efficient fine-tuning, but the study does not test whether a small set of parameters or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study proposes a data-weighting defense and discusses mechanisms of harmful fine-tuning, but does not test why safety behaviour would be shallow.
The study does not train or evaluate safety across response-token positions or test whether safety deepening persists.
